Today, I met with Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, the world's leading designer of AI chips and accelerated computing platforms. We discussed the future of AI policy and export controls. This week, I wrote a letter to Secretary of Commerce Lutnick calling on him to withdraw BIS Rule 00636, a rule that would prevent American companies from selling advanced technology to growing markets.

I recently led a bipartisan letter with some of my colleagues asking Commerce Secretary Lutnick to withdraw or fundamentally restructure the Biden administration's B.I.S. Rule 00636.

I am so thankful to have an administration in office that will listen to sound reason and judgment. This rule would have imposed sweeping export controls on integrated circuits above specific performance benchmarks.

AI isn't a future concept. It's already here.

The VA is using AI to identify veterans at elevated suicide risk before a crisis hits.

Mayo Clinic built a model that detects pancreatic cancer up to 3 years before diagnosis.

NOAA is running AI-powered hurricane forecasts that get there faster and more accurately.

I've watched this technology go from theory to lives saved. The question isn't whether AI will affect Americans. It already is. The question is whether Washington will get out of the way and let it work.

Data centers are critical to America’s future and global leadership. They power our economy, drive innovation, and help us stay ahead in the AI race.

Our adversaries would love nothing more than for America to fear progress and fall behind. I’d rather see us embrace innovation, build here at home, and keep America the global standard for technology.

People across my district keep asking me the same question: “Is AI going to take my job?”
 
It is a fair question, and hardworking Americans deserve clarity.
 
AI will create more opportunity than it displaces, from medicine and manufacturing to the skilled trades. Every great technological revolution has created disruption, before leading to decades and centuries of new prosperity.
 
The answer is not for Congress to rush in with sweeping new regulations that pick winners and losers, kill American innovation, and hand China an advantage.
 
Our job is to enforce the rules already on the books, protect Americans, and give the private sector room to build, compete, and keep the United States ahead of our adversaries. 
 
America should lead the AI revolution, not regulate itself out of it.

This week, President Trump is hosting President Xi of China for a high stakes summit. 
 
There is a lot to discuss. Trade. Taiwan. Rare earths. AI. And what the future of the U.S.-China relationship looks like.
 
Around 21% of global trade passes through the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced AI chips.
 
The stakes for American economic and national security could not be higher. These conversations matter, and America must negotiate from a position of strength.
